q: An agent advertises "Great 3-bed for sale, call 702-555-0101" with no brokerage named. This is a:
wrong: Bait and switch advertises something unavailable to lure buyers.
Puffing is exaggerated opinion.
A net listing is a type of listing agreement.
why: An ad that hides that a licensee or brokerage is behind it is a blind ad.
hook: Name the brokerage. Tell the truth.

q: An agent keeps advertising an underpriced home that already sold, to draw calls and pitch other listings. This is:
wrong: Steering is a fair housing violation.
Commingling involves money.
A tie-in conditions one purchase on another.
why: Advertising property that isn't available to lure prospects is bait and switch.
hook: Advertise what's real.

q: Before cold calling homeowners, an agent must generally:
options: Check the numbers against the National Do Not Call Registry
Get the broker to make the calls
Call only between 7 a.m. and 11 p.m.
wrong: The broker doesn't have to place the calls personally.
The permitted window is narrower: 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. local time.
No prior letter is required.
why: Telemarketers must scrub call lists against the registry unless an exception applies.
hook: Check the list. Get consent. Let them opt out.

q: Federal telemarketing rules allow calls to consumers only between:
wrong: Too wide.
Too narrow; that's not the federal window.
Weekends aren't an exception.
why: Telemarketing calls are limited to 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. in the called person's time zone.
hook: Eight to nine, or don't dial.

q: Under CAN-SPAM, a marketing email must include:
options: A working way to opt out and a valid physical postal address
A government license number for the sender
wrong: CAN-SPAM doesn't require prior consent for email, but requires an opt-out.
No license number is required by CAN-SPAM.
No attachment is required.
why: Commercial email needs honest headers, an opt-out that's honored promptly, and a physical address.
hook: Check the list. Get consent. Let them opt out.

q: Which person on the Do Not Call Registry may an agent most likely call?
options: A client whose home the agent helped buy 6 months ago
A stranger whose number came from a purchased list
A homeowner whose listing expired with another broker
A neighbor of a recent sale
wrong: No relationship exists.
The expired listing was with someone else; there's no relationship.
Proximity doesn't create a relationship.
why: An established business relationship, like a recent transaction, is an exception for a limited time.
hook: A real relationship opens the door, for a while.

q: Who is responsible for supervising a salesperson's advertising?
wrong: The MLS doesn't supervise licensees' ads.
The seller isn't responsible for licensee conduct.
Platforms don't supervise license law compliance.
why: Brokers must supervise all advertising done under the brokerage.
hook: The broker answers for the team.

q: You want to post a new listing on your personal social media account. What should the agent do?
options: Include the brokerage information required by law and office policy and make sure every claim is accurate
Post it without the brokerage so it feels personal
Exaggerate the size to get attention
Post someone else's listing as your own
wrong: Omitting required brokerage info can make it a blind ad.
False facts are misrepresentation.
Advertising others' listings without permission is misleading.
why: Social media posts are advertising. Identify the brokerage and stay accurate.
hook: Name the brokerage. Tell the truth.

q: A listing posted on an agent's social media page counts as advertising.
wrong: Advertising rules apply regardless of the medium.
why: True.
hook: Any medium, same rules.

q: Autodialed marketing text messages to cell phones generally require the recipient's prior consent.
wrong: The TCPA treats texts like calls and generally requires consent for autodialed marketing.
why: True.
hook: Check the list. Get consent.

q: A seller lowered the price, but the agent's ads still show the old, higher price. The agent should:
options: Update all ads promptly so the price is accurate
Remove the price from all ads permanently
wrong: Outdated prices mislead the public.
All ads should be accurate, not just the MLS.
Removing information isn't the fix; accuracy is.
why: Ads must be kept accurate and current.
hook: Advertise what's real.

q: A past client clicks "unsubscribe" on your monthly market email. You should:
options: Stop sending them marketing email promptly, within the time CAN-SPAM allows
Keep sending because they're a past client
Send one more email asking why
Move them to your text message list instead
wrong: Being a past client doesn't override an opt-out.
Further marketing email after opt-out isn't allowed.
Texting without consent can violate the TCPA.
why: Opt-out requests must be honored promptly; CAN-SPAM allows up to 10 business days.
hook: Let them opt out, and mean it.

q: A team may advertise using only its team name, without showing its brokerage.
wrong: Team ads generally must identify the brokerage, as state rules set out.
why: False.
hook: Name the brokerage. Tell the truth.

q: The core rule for real estate advertising is that it must be:
wrong: MLS approval isn't required.
No particular medium is required.
Puffing opinions are allowed; false facts aren't.
why: Advertising must be accurate and not misleading.
hook: Advertise what's real.

q: An agent wants to send listing flyers by fax to businesses that never asked for them. Generally:
options: Unsolicited advertising faxes are restricted by federal law
It's allowed for commercial property only
wrong: Federal law restricts unsolicited ad faxes.
Time of day doesn't change the rule.
There's no general commercial exception.
why: The TCPA, as amended, restricts unsolicited advertising faxes.
hook: No consent, no fax.

q: Real estate commission rates are:
options: Negotiable between each broker and client
wrong: No law sets commission rates.
Boards can't set rates; that would be price fixing.
The MLS can't set rates.
why: Commissions are always negotiable.
hook: Every commission is negotiable.

q: Brokers from competing firms agree at a meeting that none of them will list for less than 6%. This is:
wrong: Market allocation divides territories or customers.
A tie-in conditions one service on another.
A boycott refuses to deal with someone.
why: Competitors agreeing on rates is price fixing, a Sherman Act violation.
hook: Never talk rates with the competition.

q: Several brokers agree not to show listings of a new discount brokerage. This is:
wrong: No prices were agreed.
Steering is a fair housing violation.
Puffing is opinion in ads.
why: Competitors agreeing to shut out a firm is a group boycott.
hook: Don't fix, boycott, divide, or tie.

q: Two brokerages agree that one will handle homes over $1 million and the other homes under $1 million. This is:
wrong: Agreements between competitors to divide markets are illegal.
No purchase is tied to another.
No rates were agreed.
why: Dividing customers or price ranges among competitors is market allocation.
hook: Don't fix, boycott, divide, or tie.

q: A developer-broker will sell a lot only to buyers who agree to list their current home with the broker. This is:
wrong: Nothing is divided among competitors.
No one is being shut out by competitors.
An option is a right to buy.
why: Conditioning one sale on buying another service is a tie-in.
hook: Don't fix, boycott, divide, or tie.

q: Under the Sherman Act, an individual convicted of a criminal antitrust violation can face:
options: Fines up to $1 million and up to 10 years in prison
wrong: Antitrust violations are serious crimes.
Criminal penalties go beyond licensing.
Penalties are much larger.
why: Individuals face up to $1 million in fines and 10 years in prison; corporations up to $100 million.
hook: Antitrust: million-dollar mistakes.

q: At a networking lunch, competing agents start agreeing on what "everyone should charge." What should the agent do?
options: Object, leave the conversation, and make it clear you set your fees independently
Agree, since it helps the industry
wrong: Silence while others agree can look like participation.
Agreeing makes you part of price fixing.
Sharing invites an agreement.
why: Even appearing to join a price discussion is risky. Leave and make your independence clear.
hook: Never talk rates with the competition.

q: A broker may set their own firm's commission policy independently.
wrong: Setting your own prices independently is legal; agreeing with competitors isn't.
why: True.
hook: Your rate is your decision alone.

q: Telling a seller, "The standard commission here is 6%," is a safe statement.
wrong: Implying a standard rate suggests rates aren't negotiable and can look like price fixing.
why: False. There's no standard rate; say what your firm charges and that it's negotiable.
hook: Every commission is negotiable.

q: Which federal law is the primary source of antitrust rules for real estate brokers?
wrong: RESPA covers settlement procedures.
The FHA covers discrimination.
TILA covers credit disclosures.
why: The Sherman Act prohibits agreements in restraint of trade.
hook: Sherman stops the scheming.

q: A seller mentions a discount brokerage. Which response best avoids antitrust problems?
options: "Here's what our firm offers and charges. You can compare and decide."
"No one in town will show your home if you list there."
"We all agreed not to work with them."
wrong: Predicting a boycott can suggest one exists.
That admits a group boycott.
A false claim about a competitor is misrepresentation.
why: Compete on your own value and fees. Never imply collective action against a competitor.
hook: Compete on value, not collusion.

q: Salespeople at the same brokerage following the broker's fee policy are not engaged in price fixing.
wrong: One firm setting its own policy isn't an agreement among competitors.
why: True. Price fixing requires an agreement among competitors.
hook: Your rate is your decision alone.

q: A person harmed by an antitrust violation may sue and recover:
options: Up to three times their actual damages
Nothing; only the government can act
wrong: Antitrust law allows treble damages.
That's not a remedy.
Private suits are allowed.
why: Private antitrust plaintiffs can recover treble damages.
hook: Triple damages, triple trouble.

q: Two agents from different firms agree, "You take the north side of town, I'll take the south." This is:
wrong: Referral networks don't divide markets.
Dividing territories eliminates competition.
Designated agency is about representation within one firm.
why: Competitors dividing territories is market allocation.
hook: Don't fix, boycott, divide, or tie.

q: Price fixing is illegal even if the agreed prices are reasonable.
wrong: Price fixing is illegal per se; reasonableness is no defense.
why: True.
hook: Never talk rates with the competition.

q: Which best describes a salesperson working as an independent contractor?
options: Paid on results, controls their own methods, pays their own taxes
Required to work set office hours
wrong: That describes an employee.
Set hours point toward employee status.
Benefits point toward employee status.
why: Independent contractors are paid by results and control how they work.
hook: Paid by results, not by hours.

q: For the IRS to treat a real estate agent as a statutory nonemployee, which is required?
options: A license, pay based on sales rather than hours, and a written contract saying they aren't treated as an employee for taxes
Working fewer than 20 hours a week
wrong: Hours aren't the test.
No entity is required.
Cash payment isn't a test and isn't allowed outside the broker anyway.
why: The IRS test: licensed, paid on output, and a written contract stating non-employee tax treatment.
hook: License, results, written contract.

q: Even though salespeople are independent contractors for tax purposes, the broker must still:
options: Supervise their real estate activities as license law requires
wrong: Contractors pay their own taxes.
Controlling hours suggests employment.
Benefits aren't required for contractors.
why: Tax status doesn't change the broker's duty to supervise under license law.
hook: Contractor for taxes, supervised by law.

q: A salesperson may receive compensation for real estate work from:
options: The seller directly, if the seller insists
wrong: Payments from others must go through the broker.
Even the seller must pay through the broker.
Title companies don't pay licensees for brokerage work.
why: All compensation flows through the employing broker.
hook: All pay flows through the broker.

q: Your happy buyer offers you a $1,000 cash bonus at closing. What should the agent do?
options: Explain it must be paid through your broker and handled as required, and check office policy
Ask for a check made out to you personally
Ask them to give it to your spouse
wrong: Payment outside the broker violates license law.
Still bypasses the broker.
Routing it through others is still improper.
why: Compensation for real estate work must go through your broker.
hook: All pay flows through the broker.

q: A broker can be held responsible for the acts of salespeople working under them.
wrong: Brokers are responsible for supervising, and can share liability.
why: True.
hook: The broker answers for the team.

q: An unlicensed assistant may negotiate price with buyers if the agent is busy.
wrong: Negotiating is licensed activity. Unlicensed assistants are limited to clerical and administrative tasks.
why: False.
hook: No license, no negotiating.

q: Which task can an unlicensed assistant usually do?
options: Show property and answer questions about price
wrong: Showing and discussing price is licensed activity.
Explaining contracts is licensed activity.
Negotiating is licensed activity.
why: Unlicensed assistants handle clerical tasks only.
hook: No license, no negotiating.

q: A broker receives a $15,000 commission on a sale. The salesperson's agreement gives them 70%. How much does the salesperson receive?
hook: All pay flows through the broker, then splits.

q: If a brokerage treats a salesperson as an employee, the brokerage generally must:
options: Pay the salesperson only on closed deals
Pay them through the title company
wrong: Employees can be paid other ways; withholding is the key obligation.
Supervision is still required.
Pay always flows through the broker.
why: Employers withhold taxes for employees.
hook: Employee: taxes withheld.

q: Why should a brokerage have a written independent contractor agreement with each salesperson?
options: It's part of the IRS test and documents duties, splits, and supervision
It lets salespeople pay themselves directly
wrong: Nothing replaces the license.
Pay still flows through the broker.
The broker stays responsible under license law.
why: The written agreement supports tax status and sets expectations.
hook: License, results, written contract.

q: You're unsure whether a contract addendum is filled out correctly. What should the agent do?
options: Ask your broker or designated supervisor before it goes out
Send it and hope for the best
Ask the other agent to fix it
Have your client fill it in
wrong: Guessing on contracts creates risk for your client.
The other agent represents the other side.
Shifting your job to the client isn't appropriate.
why: Use your broker's supervision. That's what it's for.
hook: When in doubt, ask your broker.

q: A salesperson may operate a brokerage independently without being supervised by a broker.
wrong: Salespeople must work under a licensed broker.
why: False.
hook: Salesperson works through the broker.

q: A broker's supervision typically covers:
options: Advertising, contracts, trust funds, and licensee conduct
wrong: Supervision is broader.
Supervision is broader.
Splits are a business matter, not the whole duty.
why: Brokers supervise all real estate activity of their licensees.
hook: The broker answers for the team.

q: A salesperson leaves a brokerage while a deal they worked on is still pending. Any commission they're owed on it is generally paid:
options: By the former broker, according to their agreement
wrong: Clients don't pay salespeople directly.
The new broker wasn't involved.
Earned pay may still be owed under the agreement.
why: The original broker earned the commission and pays the salesperson under their agreement.
hook: All pay flows through the broker.

q: Errors and omissions insurance generally covers:
wrong: E&O doesn't cover intentional wrongdoing.
Fines for crimes aren't covered.
That's auto insurance.
why: E&O covers honest professional mistakes, not fraud.
hook: E&O covers errors, not lies.

q: A buyer receives an email that appears to be from the title company with "updated wiring instructions." The buyer should:
options: Call the title company at a known, independently verified number before wiring
Wire immediately to avoid delaying closing
Reply to the email to confirm
Call the number in the email
wrong: Speed is what scammers count on.
Replying goes straight to the scammer.
The number in a fake email reaches the scammer.
why: Always verify wiring instructions by calling a known number, never one in the email.
hook: Never trust a wire email. Call a known number.

q: When should you warn clients about wire fraud?
options: At the start of the transaction, and again before closing
Never, it's the title company's job
wrong: Many don't know to ask.
By then the money may be gone.
Everyone in the transaction has a role in prevention.
why: Early and repeated warnings are the best defense.
hook: Warn early, warn again.

q: Which is a sound risk-management practice?
options: Documenting important conversations and decisions in writing
Giving legal advice to save clients money
Skipping disclosures to keep deals simple
wrong: Legal advice is outside a licensee's role.
Approved, tested forms reduce risk.
Skipped disclosures create liability.
why: Written records protect clients and the licensee.
hook: Write it down, and refer what you don't know.

q: Which is true about a professional association's Code of Ethics?
options: It binds the association's members and can be stricter than license law
It's the same as state license law
It binds every licensee in the state
It's enforced by the Real Estate Division
wrong: License law is enacted by the state.
It applies only to members.
The association enforces its own code.
why: Codes of Ethics are association rules for members; license law comes from the state.
hook: Law is the floor. Ethics can raise the bar.

q: Brokers must keep transaction records for the period state law requires.
wrong: Record retention periods are set by state law.
why: True. Nevada's period is covered in the state units.
hook: Keep it as long as the law says.

q: E&O insurance will protect a licensee who knowingly hides a defect.
wrong: Intentional misconduct is excluded from E&O coverage.
why: False.
hook: E&O covers errors, not lies.

q: Which is the safest way to handle clients' sensitive documents, like bank statements?
options: Use your brokerage's secure document system and limit who can access them
Keep them in a public cloud folder anyone can open
Text them to your personal phone
wrong: Open folders expose private data.
Personal devices without controls raise exposure.
Printing extras multiplies the risk.
why: Protect client data with secure, limited-access systems.
hook: Private data, private place.

q: You discover your email account was hacked during an active transaction. What should the agent do?
options: Tell your broker, the title or escrow company, and your clients immediately, and warn them not to trust any emailed wiring instructions
Change the password and say nothing
Wait to see if anything happens
wrong: Silence leaves clients exposed to fraud.
Waiting can cost clients their closing funds.
Deleting the account doesn't warn anyone and may destroy records.
why: A compromised email is a wire-fraud emergency. Alert everyone right away.
hook: Hacked? Warn everyone, now.

q: Why do brokerages use standard, approved contract forms?
options: To reduce errors and avoid licensees drafting legal language
wrong: Handwritten terms can be valid; the issue is legal drafting by non-lawyers.
Forms don't set commissions.
Forms often include disclosures.
why: Approved forms keep licensees from practicing law and reduce mistakes.
hook: Fill in forms; don't write law.

q: A client asks whether a 1031 exchange makes sense for them. The best response is:
options: Explain it's a tax question and recommend a CPA or tax attorney
Say yes, it always saves taxes
wrong: That's tax advice, and not always true.
That's also tax advice.
Exchanges involve specialized tax and legal work.
why: Tax advice belongs with tax professionals.
hook: Know your lane. Refer the rest.

q: State license law sets the legal minimum standards for licensee conduct.
wrong: License law is the floor everyone must meet.
why: True.
hook: Law is the floor.

q: Which is a common sign of a wire-fraud email?
options: Urgent request to wire to a new account, from an address that's slightly off
A greeting with the client's name
wrong: Scammers often know names from hacked accounts.
Attachments alone aren't a sign.
Timing alone isn't a sign.
why: Last-minute account changes and look-alike addresses are classic red flags.
hook: New account + urgency = stop and call.

q: An agent notices a typo in the purchase price that favors their client by $10,000. The ethical step is:
options: Point out the error so the documents reflect the actual agreement
Say nothing because it benefits the client
wrong: Taking advantage of a known mistake isn't honest dealing.
The documents must reflect the real agreement for everyone.
Waiting makes the problem worse.
why: Honesty and fair dealing mean correcting known errors.
hook: Honest with everyone.

q: Relying on verbal agreements for repairs reduces risk because there's less paperwork to get wrong.
wrong: Verbal agreements are hard to prove. Put agreements in writing.
why: False.
hook: Write it down.
